title: GitOps with Argo CD
intro: In Part 10 you deployed hello-devops to Kubernetes by typing commands yourself. In this part a program called Argo CD takes over that job: git holds the plan, and Argo CD keeps the cluster equal to it, all day long. First you install it and watch it undo a hand edit and roll back a bad release. Then you run the app as a test copy and a live copy, and move a version between them with a pull request. Along the way you see how teams handle new versions, secrets and access.

lessons.title: GitOps with Argo CD
lessons.goal: By the end you can install Argo CD on your kind cluster, let it deploy hello-devops from your GitHub repo, and fix drift and roll back using only git.

guess.q: A program called Argo CD deploys your app from git, the tool that keeps the history of your files. It runs with its default settings. A teammate then changes the running app by hand with a quick command. What happens to that hand edit?
options: Argo CD undoes it within a few seconds
It stays, and Argo CD shows the app as OutOfSync
kubectl refuses the edit, because git owns the app
Argo CD copies the change back into git
guess.why: By default Argo CD only reports the difference. Undoing hand edits is a separate setting called self-heal, and it stays off until you turn it on.

sections.h: Why deploying from your own laptop stops working
sections.body:
Software has the same problem. Kubernetes is the system that runs your app on a group of machines, called a cluster, and keeps it running. All through Part 10 you ran hello-devops there. It is the tiny web app from the lab that answers every visit with a greeting and a count of visits so far.

You told the cluster what to run with one command from your laptop: `kubectl apply -k k8s`. kubectl is the command line tool that sends your wishes to Kubernetes. The folder `k8s` holds YAML files, plain text files that describe what should run. For one person, that is fine: one cook writes the board and cooks the food. Add a few colleagues, and it breaks in quiet ways:
- Someone fixes the app by hand at night and never updates the files.
- Two people apply different versions of the files, and the last one wins.
- Nobody can say which version of the files is running right now.
- Every laptop or pipeline that deploys holds a key that can change the cluster.

A difference between the files and what really runs is called drift. You met it on Day 33 with Terraform, the tool that builds servers from code: it noticed a hand change only when you ran `plan` again.

GitOps closes that gap from the other side. Git is the tool that keeps every saved version of your files. Each saved version is a commit, and the folder with all that history is a repo. With GitOps, git becomes the only place where changes happen. A program inside the cluster keeps the cluster equal to git, all the time. In restaurant terms, git is the board, the cluster is the dining room, and that program is the floor manager.

The [OpenGitOps project](https://opengitops.dev/), part of the CNCF (the foundation behind Kubernetes), sums this up in four principles. The desired state, meaning what you want running, must be:
- Declarative: you describe what you want, not the steps to get there.
- Versioned and immutable: it is stored with its full history, and old versions never change.
- Pulled automatically: software agents fetch it by themselves.
- Continuously reconciled: agents keep comparing the real system with it and fix differences.

The last one should feel familiar. On Day 38 you watched controllers, small programs in the cluster, do exactly that. GitOps runs the same loop one level up, with git as the thing you asked for.

**A change that is not in git did not happen. Put every change in git.**

So who carries a change from git into the cluster? There are two answers.

sections.h: Who carries the change: push deploys and pull deploys
sections.body:
A restaurant owner could phone in each change from home, or a manager could read the board every few minutes. Deploys come in the same two styles.

In a push deploy, something outside the cluster sends the change in. Usually that is a CI pipeline, the automatic build and test steps from Part 6 that run every time you push code to GitHub. The pipeline ends with `kubectl apply`, so the pipeline holds a key that can write to the cluster. Any workflow that can read that secret can change production, the real system your users depend on. And if someone edits the cluster after the pipeline ends, nothing notices.

In a pull deploy, an agent (a program that does its job on its own) runs inside the cluster. It reads git and applies what it finds. CI builds the image (the packaged app, from Part 5) and changes a file in git, and that is all CI does. The pull model gives you:
- No cluster keys in CI, because the agent already lives in the cluster.
- A deploy log at no extra cost: `git log` shows who changed what, and when.
- Review before deploy, because every change can be a pull request (Part 6), a change that a teammate approves first.
- Rollback with `git revert`.
- Drift detection all day, even when nobody is deploying.

The price of the pull model is one more system to learn and keep upgraded. On your laptop it is seven extra Pods. A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that live together. For any cluster that more than one person touches, I think the pull model is worth that price.

CI still tests the code and builds the image. GitOps replaces only the last step, the one that touches the cluster.

Our agent is Argo CD. Next, we'll see what it is made of.

sections.h: What Argo CD is made of
sections.body:
Argo CD, a CNCF project, is our floor manager, and like a real manager it has a small team. It runs as a set of Pods in its own namespace, `argocd`. A namespace is a named area inside a cluster that keeps one group of things apart from the rest. After the install you will see seven Pods:
- `argocd-server`: Argo CD's own API server (a program that answers requests), behind the web page and the `argocd` tool.
- `argocd-repo-server`: copies your repo and turns a folder into plain YAML.
- `argocd-application-controller`: compares the cluster with that YAML and applies the difference.
- `argocd-applicationset-controller`: makes many Applications from one template (Day 48).
- `argocd-redis`: a cache, a fast short-term memory for rendered YAML and app state.
- `argocd-dex-server`: connects Argo CD to single sign-on, so people log in with GitHub or Google accounts.
- `argocd-notifications-controller`: sends messages, for example to the chat app Slack when a sync fails.

The repo server also understands Kustomize and Helm, two tools that build YAML from smaller pieces (Argo CD 3.5 ships with Helm 4). The application controller runs the reconcile loop. One round goes like this:
1. The controller asks the repo server for the YAML of the newest commit on the branch (a named line of commits, usually `main`).
2. The repo server fetches the repo and renders the folder into plain YAML.
3. The controller compares that YAML with the live objects. It watches them through the Kubernetes API server, the front desk for every request to the cluster.
4. It applies the difference, if the sync settings allow it, and writes the result into the Application's status.

You tell Argo CD what to deploy with an Application. It is a custom resource: a new kind of object that a tool adds to Kubernetes. It has three main parts:
- A source: the repo URL, the branch (`targetRevision`) and the folder (`path`).
- A destination: which cluster and which namespace.
- A project: rules about what this app may touch. Everything starts in the project called `default`.

How does Argo CD know which objects in the cluster are its own? Since version 3.0 it writes an annotation, a note that Kubernetes stores but does not act on, on every object it applies: `argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id`. Older versions used a label (a similar tag), and many blog posts still say so. The worked example shows one.

Next, we'll install the whole team on your laptop.

sections.h: Installing Argo CD on kind, and the flag old videos miss
sections.body:
kind, from Part 10, runs a small Kubernetes cluster inside Docker on your laptop. Installing Argo CD there means applying one long YAML file (see the Commands list). Two of its flags look odd, and older videos leave them out. Their plain `kubectl apply -n argocd -f install.yaml` fails on Argo CD 3.x with an error about annotations that are too long.

Here is why. Normal apply, called client-side apply, stores a full copy of each object in an annotation, so it can compare next time. Annotations on one object are limited to 262 KB in total. One of Argo CD's custom resource definitions, the one for ApplicationSets, is too big for that. A custom resource definition is the file that teaches Kubernetes a new kind of object.

The fix is `kubectl apply --server-side`. It lets the API server work out the changes, and it keeps no such copy. The second flag, `--force-conflicts`, lets the install take over fields that an earlier apply set, which matters when you upgrade.

The install URL points at the `stable` branch, which is fine on a laptop. At work you pin a version, with a tag such as `v3.5.6` in the URL instead of `stable`. A tag is a fixed name for one exact commit. Then every install gives the same result.

Argo CD's web page is not reachable from outside the cluster, because its Service, `argocd-server`, is a ClusterIP (Day 41). A Service gives Pods one stable address, and a ClusterIP address works only inside the cluster. On a laptop, `kubectl port-forward` is the simplest way in. It opens a port on your laptop, a numbered door for network traffic, and passes everything through to the Service. Use local port 8443, because 8080 may still be busy from your Terraform work in Part 8.

Expect a warning in the browser. The install makes its own certificate (the proof a website shows that it is who it says it is), and your browser has never heard of a self-signed one.

Log in as `admin` with the password from `argocd admin initial-password -n argocd`. Out of the box, `admin` is the only user, and it may do everything; Day 48 shows how teams give people narrower roles. Install the `argocd` CLI (a tool you type commands into) with Homebrew, the Mac's installer for such tools, and log it in through the same port-forward.

Next, we'll read the two status words that the web page shows for each app.

sections.h: Two statuses: does it match, and does it work
sections.body:
The floor manager asks two things about each table: does it match the board, and are the guests happy? If the board is wrong, a table can match it and still have unhappy guests. Every Argo CD Application shows the same two statuses, and beginners often read them as one.

Sync status answers one question: does the cluster match git?
- `Synced`: every object Argo CD manages matches the YAML in git.
- `OutOfSync`: at least one object differs, is missing, or should be gone.

Health answers a different question: does it work? Our example is a Deployment, the Kubernetes object that keeps a set number of copies of your app running. Each copy is called a replica.
- `Healthy`: for a Deployment, all replicas are updated and available.
- `Progressing`: not healthy yet but still moving, such as a rollout (a switch to a new version) in progress.
- `Degraded`: failed, for example a rollout that ran past its deadline.
- `Missing`: in git, but not in the cluster yet.
- `Suspended` and `Unknown` show up less often.

The two are independent. Push a typo in an image tag, the version name of the image, and the app is Synced but not Healthy. The cluster has exactly what git says, but the new Pods cannot pull an image that does not exist. Make a hand edit to a label, and the app is OutOfSync but still Healthy. The health of a whole app is the worst health of its parts.

How fast does Argo CD see a new commit? By default it checks git about every three minutes: 120 seconds plus a random delay of up to 60 seconds, so that many apps do not all ask at once. Press Refresh in the web page, or run `argocd app get hello-devops --refresh`, to check now.

Teams whose Argo CD has a public address add a git webhook, a message GitHub sends the moment you push. GitHub cannot reach your kind cluster, so here you wait or press Refresh. Changes inside the cluster are different. The controller watches the objects it manages, so it sees a `kubectl edit` (a change typed straight into a live object) within seconds.

Seeing a difference is only half the job. Next, we'll decide what Argo CD should do about it.

sections.h: Letting Argo CD act: automated sync, self-heal and prune
sections.body:
Out of the box, Argo CD is a manager who only takes notes. You press Sync, in the web page or with `argocd app sync`, and it applies git. Automated sync applies new commits by itself. Two more switches decide how strict it is:
- `selfHeal: true` undoes changes made in the cluster but not in git, such as a `kubectl edit`.
- `prune: true` deletes objects you removed from git. Without it, they stay, and Argo CD only marks them for pruning.

Both are off by default, a careful choice for a tool that can delete things. Remember your guess? With the default settings, the hand edit stays, and the app only shows OutOfSync. Automated sync alone does not change that. The lab's `argocd/application.yaml` turns both switches on.

Self-heal gets tricky because Argo CD is not the only controller that changes your objects. On Day 43 you added a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA). It is a controller that adds replicas when the app is busy and removes them when it is quiet. Under load, the HPA sets 5 replicas where git says 3. Argo CD sees the difference and, with self-heal on, sets it back. The HPA raises it again. They fight for as long as the load lasts. In the restaurant, it is the manager sending home the extra waiters that the head waiter just called in for a rush.

There are two ways out:
- Leave `replicas` out of the Deployment in git, so there is nothing to compare. The [Argo CD best practices](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/best_practices/) page suggests this.
- Tell Argo CD to ignore that one field. The lab does this with `ignoreDifferences` on `/spec/replicas`.

The sync option `RespectIgnoreDifferences=true` makes a sync leave the field alone too. The lab takes the second way so that `k8s/deployment.yaml` keeps `replicas: 3`, and `kubectl apply -k k8s` still works without Argo CD.

**Two controllers fighting over one field never stop. Give each field one owner.**

Self-heal protects git from hand edits. But what if the mistake is in git itself? Next, we'll roll back.

sections.body:
Sooner or later, a bad change gets through. With GitOps, a rollback is a commit. You undo the bad change in git, and Argo CD deploys the state from before:
1. `git log --oneline -3` shows the recent commits, each with a short id called a sha.
2. `git revert <sha>` makes a new commit that undoes the bad one. History stays intact.
3. `git push`, then wait for the next check or run `argocd app sync hello-devops`.

You may be thinking, "Why not `kubectl rollout undo` from Day 40? It is one command." It changes the cluster but not git, so with self-heal on, Argo CD puts the bad version straight back. Our manager is loyal to the board, even when the board is wrong.

Argo CD has its own `argocd app rollback` command, which redeploys an earlier entry from `argocd app history`. It refuses to run while automated sync is on, for the same reason: git must stay the source of truth.

In a real emergency, follow this order:
1. Turn off automated sync for that one app.
2. Fix the cluster by hand, and write down every change.
3. Put the same fix into git.
4. Turn automated sync back on.

Skip step 3, and the next sync quietly undoes your fix.

All of this works for one app in one place. Real teams keep a test copy and a live copy of each app, and one Application cannot move a version safely from one to the other. The next lesson picks up there.

steps.say: Start from where the task below ends: Argo CD runs on your kind cluster and deploys hello-devops with self-heal on. An Application is an ordinary Kubernetes object, so kubectl can list it, with both statuses.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n argocd get applications
NAME           SYNC STATUS   HEALTH STATUS
hello-devops   Synced        Healthy

steps.say: See how Argo CD marks what it owns. Every object it applied carries a tracking annotation, its name tag. The tag holds the app name, then the object's group and kind (its family and type), then its namespace and name. A ConfigMap is a small object that holds settings, such as the greeting. It belongs to the core group, whose name is empty, so nothing stands before the slash.

Now play the colleague who fixes things by hand. Change the greeting in the live ConfigMap and skip git. A `kubectl scale` would make a poor demo, because the lab tells Argo CD to ignore the replica count.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello patch configmap hello-config --type merge \
    -p '{"data":{"GREETING":"Edited by hand"}}'
configmap/hello-config patched

steps.say: The application controller watches every object it manages, so it sees the change at once. If you are quick, you catch the app OutOfSync. It stays Healthy, because the app still runs fine. Self-heal then puts git's version back after a short pause.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n argocd get applications
NAME           SYNC STATUS   HEALTH STATUS
hello-devops   OutOfSync     Healthy

steps.say: Wait a few seconds and read the value again. Git's text is back, and you did nothing.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello get configmap hello-config -o jsonpath='{.data.GREETING}'
Hello from Kubernetes!

steps.say: To change the greeting for good, change git. Edit `k8s/configmap.yaml`, commit and push, then sync instead of waiting up to three minutes. Pods read their settings (environment variables) only when they start (Day 42), so restart the Deployment to see the new text.
steps.code:
$ git commit -am "Change the greeting"
$ git push
$ argocd app sync hello-devops
$ kubectl -n hello rollout restart deployment hello-devops

code.title: argocd/application.yaml
code.src:
# An Argo CD Application: "keep the cluster equal to the k8s/ folder in git".
# Apply it once:  kubectl apply -n argocd -f argocd/application.yaml
# Replace <your-github-user> with your GitHub user name first.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  # Applications live in the namespace where Argo CD runs.
  namespace: argocd
  # When you delete this Application, also delete the things it created.
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
spec:
  project: default
  # Where the desired state lives: your repo, branch main, folder k8s.
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/<your-github-user>/hello-devops
    targetRevision: main
    path: k8s
  # Where to deploy: the same cluster Argo CD runs in, namespace hello.
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: hello
  # The autoscaler (k8s/hpa.yaml) changes the number of replicas while the app runs.
  # Ignore that one field, so Argo CD and the autoscaler do not fight.
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      name: hello-devops
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true # delete things that you removed from git
      selfHeal: true # undo changes made by hand in the cluster
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true # create namespace hello if it is missing
      - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true # also skip /spec/replicas when syncing

task.title: Put hello-devops under GitOps
steps: Start your kind cluster from Day 38 if it is not running (`kind get clusters` should list `devops`). Push your latest `k8s/` folder to GitHub.
Install Argo CD with the first two commands in the Commands list. Wait until all seven Pods in namespace `argocd` show Running.

explain_back.prompt: Explain GitOps to a teammate in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention who applies changes, what self-heal does, and how you roll back.
explain_back.answer: With GitOps, git holds the desired state of the cluster, and an agent inside the cluster, here Argo CD, applies it. Nobody runs kubectl apply by hand. A change is a commit, usually through a pull request, and CI never needs a cluster key. Argo CD keeps comparing the cluster with git, and self-heal undoes changes that skipped git. To roll back, you revert the commit, and Argo CD deploys the old state.

recap: GitOps: git holds the desired state, and an agent in the cluster pulls it and keeps the cluster equal to it.
Pull deploys keep cluster keys out of CI, and git gives you review, history and rollback.
An Application links a repo folder to a cluster and namespace. Install Argo CD 3.x with server-side apply.
Sync status says whether the cluster matches git; health says whether it works. They are independent.
Self-heal undoes hand edits and prune deletes what left git; both are off by default. Give each field one owner, so ignore HPA replicas.
Roll back with git revert. One Application covers one app in one place; moving a version from test to live needs more (next lesson).

check.q: The hello-devops app shows Synced and Degraded. What does that tell you?
options: The cluster matches git, but what git describes does not work
Someone edited the cluster by hand since the last sync
Argo CD cannot reach your GitHub repo right now
Prune is off, so old objects are still in the cluster
check.why: Synced means the cluster equals git. Degraded means the objects fail, so the problem is in what you committed, such as a bad image tag.

check.q: You delete `redis.yaml` from git and push. Automated sync is on, but prune is off. What happens to Redis in the cluster?
options: It is deleted at the next sync
Argo CD puts redis.yaml back into your repo
It keeps running, and Argo CD marks it for pruning
The sync fails and nothing else deploys
check.why: Without prune, automated sync never deletes anything. The object stays, flagged as no longer in git, until someone prunes it.

check.q: A bad release is live, and self-heal is on. A colleague runs `kubectl rollout undo` (Day 40) to fix it fast. What happens next?
options: The rollback stays until the next commit
Argo CD writes the older version into git
The Deployment is deleted and created again
Argo CD puts the bad version back, because git still says so
check.why: Self-heal makes the cluster match git, and git still holds the bad version. Revert in git instead.

interview.q: What is GitOps, and how is it different from a CI pipeline that runs kubectl apply?
interview.a: GitOps keeps the desired state of a system in git, and an agent such as Argo CD or Flux pulls it and keeps the system equal to it. A push pipeline runs kubectl apply from outside, so it needs cluster credentials, and it only acts while it runs. The GitOps agent runs inside the cluster, keeps reconciling, and can undo drift. Every change is a commit, so review, history and rollback come from normal git tools.

interview.q: How do you roll back a bad deploy in an Argo CD setup?
interview.a: I revert the commit, or the pull request, that introduced the change and push, so git again describes the last good state. Argo CD syncs, and the cluster follows. Argo CD has its own rollback command, but it refuses to run while automated sync is on, and it would leave the cluster different from git. A git revert keeps one source of truth and leaves a clear record of who changed what.

interview.q: What do sync status and health status mean in Argo CD?
interview.a: Sync status compares the cluster with git: Synced means they match, OutOfSync means something differs. Health says whether the objects work, for example whether a Deployment's replicas are updated and available. They are independent. A bad image tag gives Synced but Degraded, and a harmless hand edit gives OutOfSync but Healthy. I check both before I call a deploy done.

deeper.body:
On Day 38 you saw that a controller has to know which objects are its own. A ReplicaSet, the object a Deployment uses to keep its Pods running, does this with labels and owner references. An owner reference is a field on a Pod that names the object that made it. Argo CD has the same problem on a bigger scale. One cluster can hold objects from many Applications, plus objects that other controllers create.

Since 3.0, Argo CD tracks objects with the annotation `argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id`, in the form `app:group/Kind:namespace/name`. Before 3.0 the default was the label `app.kubernetes.io/instance`. That label caused two kinds of trouble:
- Other tools copy labels. An operator, a controller that manages one kind of software, may copy its labels onto the objects it creates. A copied label could make Argo CD think it owned those objects.
- Label values may be at most 63 characters, so long app names were cut short.

The annotation names the exact object it sits on. If a tool copies it onto a different object, the name inside no longer matches, and Argo CD ignores the copy. You can still switch to label tracking in the `argocd-cm` ConfigMap, where Argo CD keeps its main settings, but there is rarely a reason to.

Argo CD also ignores some objects on purpose. Since 3.0 its default settings exclude kinds that change all the time, such as EndpointSlice, Endpoints and Lease. An EndpointSlice is the list of Pod addresses behind a Service, so it changes every time a Pod becomes ready or not ready (Day 41). A Lease is a small object that programs renew every few seconds to show they are alive. Watching all of them would load the API server for no benefit, because nobody keeps them in git anyway.

Inside one object, Argo CD skips the `status` part by default, since the cluster writes it. You add your own exceptions with `ignoreDifferences`, as the lab does for replicas. Use it narrowly. Each ignored field is a place where git no longer tells the whole truth.

Finally, an object that lives in the app's namespace but in no Application is an orphaned resource. Argo CD never deletes it, because it never created it. A project can turn on warnings for orphaned resources with `orphanedResources`. That is a cheap way to spot leftovers from hand-made experiments, as long as the namespaces are small.

For hello-devops this all runs quietly in the background. It starts to matter when a second tool, such as a service mesh or an operator, writes to the same objects as Argo CD. A service mesh is a layer that manages traffic between apps, and Part 15 covers it. Then `ignoreDifferences` and tracking decide who wins.

lessons.opening:
Picture a small restaurant on a busy Friday night. On the kitchen wall hangs a board with tonight's plan: which dishes are on, how many cooks work the line, which tables are open. Around seven, a waiter joins two tables for a big group. A cook takes a dish off because the fish ran out. Nobody writes any of it on the board. By nine, the board and the room tell two different stories, and the next shift believes the board.

It is an easy mess to get into. Every change made sense at the time, and writing it down felt like extra work. Last time, you tracked down broken apps on your cluster and fixed them by typing commands by hand. That left a quiet question: who keeps the board and the room in step?

In this lesson, we'll hand that job to a program, watch it undo a hand edit, and roll back a bad release using nothing but the history of your files.

Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

aside.title: If the manager undoes hand edits, can I still use kubectl at all?
aside.body: Yes. Commands that only read, such as `kubectl get`, `kubectl describe` and `kubectl logs`, change nothing, so Argo CD has nothing to undo. They stay your main tools for finding problems, as they were last time. What changes is where writes go. A write to an object Argo CD manages belongs in git, or it will not last. Objects that Argo CD does not manage, such as a throwaway test Pod, are still yours to create and delete by hand.

lessons.closing:
We started with a restaurant board that nobody updated and a room that slowly drifted away from it. Now git is the board, and Argo CD is the manager. It keeps the cluster equal to git, undoes hand edits, and follows a revert back to the last good state. In your lab, open `argocd/application.yaml` and find the `ignoreDifferences` block. Then ask which other field a second controller might change behind Argo CD's back.

Next, we'll run hello-devops as two copies, dev and prod, and answer the question every team meets: how does a tested version move safely from one to the other?

lessons.title: GitOps in practice: environments, promotion and image updates
lessons.goal: By the end you can run hello-devops as dev and prod from one ApplicationSet, promote a tested version from dev to prod with a pull request, and pick a safe way to keep secrets out of a GitOps repo.

guess.q: Version 1.2.0 runs well in dev, the test copy of your app. In a GitOps setup, how do you move it to prod, the copy your users see?
options: Rebuild the image from the main branch for prod
Run `kubectl set image` in the prod namespace
Copy the 1.2.0 tag into the prod folder with a pull request
Click Sync on the prod app in the Argo CD UI
guess.why: Promotion is a change in git: prod gets the exact version that dev already runs. A rebuild could produce a slightly different app, a hand edit with kubectl gets undone, and Sync only applies what git already says.

sections.h: Where the deployment files should live
sections.body:
Before we add a second room, we have to decide where the board hangs. Right now hello-devops, the tiny web app that answers every visit with a greeting and a count, keeps everything in one repo. A repo is a folder that git tracks, with its full history. The app's code sits at the top. The YAML files that tell Kubernetes, the system that runs your app, what to run sit in `k8s/`.

Teams pick one of three layouts:
- One repo per app, with code and YAML together. This is what you have now.
- An app repo for the code, plus a separate config repo that holds only YAML for every environment.
- A monorepo: one big repo for many apps, with a folder per app and per environment.

An environment is one running copy of the app with one purpose, such as a test copy or the live copy. The first layout keeps the board inside the recipe book; the second gives it a wall of its own.

The [Argo CD best practices](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/best_practices/) page recommends the separate config repo. It gives these reasons:
- You can change a replica count (how many copies run) without a full CI build (the automatic test and build run from Part 6).
- The config history reads like a deploy log, without code commits in between.
- One config repo can deploy an app built from several code repos as one unit.
- Access can differ: many people may change code, while few may change prod.
- CI that commits YAML into the code repo can trigger itself in a loop: its own push starts CI again.

That last point needs care in GitHub Actions, the CI service you used. Each workflow gets a built-in key called `GITHUB_TOKEN`. A push made with that key does not start new workflow runs, which stops most loops. A push made with a personal token does start them.

For one person and a laptop cluster, one repo is fine, and this lesson keeps it. (Go deeper has one small cost of that choice.)

The board has a home. Next, we'll make it serve two rooms.

sections.h: Two rooms from one board: dev, prod and the ApplicationSet
sections.body:
The test kitchen has one cook and the main room has four, but they serve the same menu. Software teams keep the same pair. Dev is where new versions land first, and prod is what users see. Real teams usually give prod its own cluster, its own group of machines. Here both live in your kind cluster, in the namespaces `hello-dev` and `hello-prod`, two named areas kept apart from each other.

On Day 45 you built two Kustomize overlays, `overlays/dev` and `overlays/prod`. Kustomize is a tool that takes shared YAML and lays small changes on top. Each overlay is one such set of changes over the shared files in `k8s/`.

Dev runs one Pod (one running copy of the app) and answers "Hello from dev!". Prod runs four, with more memory and a PodDisruptionBudget, a rule that keeps enough Pods alive during maintenance. Both turn their Service, the stable address in front of the Pods, into a ClusterIP that works only inside the cluster. So they do not fight last time's app over NodePort 30080. `kubectl kustomize overlays/prod` prints exactly what prod gets.

Argo CD, the program from last time that keeps the cluster equal to git, needs one Application per environment. That is the short file saying which folder to deploy where. You could copy `application.yaml` twice and change three lines in each copy. That works until someone forgets a line. An ApplicationSet writes those copies for you. It has two parts:
- Generators produce a list of values. The lab uses the list generator with two entries, `env: dev` and `env: prod`.
- A template is an ordinary Application with placeholders such as `{{.env}}`. One of Argo CD's own programs fills it in once per entry.

In the restaurant, the template is a blank board with gaps, and the list says which words go in the gaps for each room.

Apply `argocd/applicationset.yaml`, and two Applications appear: `hello-devops-dev` and `hello-devops-prod`. Add a third entry, and a third app appears. Delete the ApplicationSet, and its Applications go too, along with everything they deployed.

Two rooms now run from one board. Next, we'll move a version from one room to the other.

sections.h: Moving a version from dev to prod with a pull request
sections.body:
Back to the soup. The restaurant's fix is simple. The test kitchen writes the exact recipe on a card, and the head chef signs it. The main kitchen cooks from that card and nothing else. Moving a version that passed in one environment on to the next is called promotion.

Two words first. An image is your app packed with everything it needs to run (Part 5). Its tag is the version label after the colon, such as `1.2.0`. In GitOps, promotion is a small text change in git:
1. CI builds `ghcr.io/<you>/hello-devops:1.2.0` once, when you push the tag `v1.2.0` (Day 27).
2. A pull request sets the dev overlay to `1.2.0`. You merge it, and Argo CD deploys dev.
3. You test dev.
4. A second pull request sets the prod overlay to the same `1.2.0`. Someone reviews and merges it, and Argo CD deploys prod.

A pull request is a proposed change that a teammate reviews. Merging it joins it to the main branch, the line of history Argo CD watches. It is the head chef's signature.

The image never gets rebuilt. Prod runs the exact bytes that dev ran, which is the build once, deploy many idea from Day 23. The pull request gives you a review and a record of who approved it. It also gives you a clean undo: the Revert button on a merged pull request opens a new one that puts the old tag back.

**A rebuilt image is a new soup with an old name. Build once, and move that same image.**

This only works if a tag always means the same image. Never deploy `latest`. It points at different images over time, so git no longer tells you what runs, and a revert cannot bring the old version back. That breaks the "versioned and immutable" principle from last time.

A version tag such as `1.2.0` is good. A digest such as `@sha256:...` is stronger. A digest is a fingerprint worked out from the image's contents, so nobody can move it to a different image. The `images` field in a kustomization accepts a `digest` too.

Next, we'll let a robot write the new tag, and see why the obvious tool makes a mess.

sections.h: Getting a new tag into git without a messy diff
sections.body:
Argo CD deploys only what git says, so something has to write each new tag into a file. Teams use two common ways.

The first is a CI job that edits the file and opens a pull request. The classic tool for the edit is `kustomize edit set image`, run inside an overlay folder. It works, but it rewrites the whole file in its own style. On the lab's prod overlay it changed 80 lines to set one tag, because it drops comments at line ends and re-indents lists. Picture a reviewer hunting for one changed word on a page that someone retyped from scratch.

So the lab's `bump-image.yml` workflow uses `yq`, a command line tool for YAML, which changes only the fields you name. You give the workflow an environment and a version, and it:
1. Checks that the version looks like `1.2.0`.
2. Sets `newName` and `newTag` of the `hello-devops` image in that environment's overlay.
3. Pushes a branch and opens a pull request with the `gh` CLI, GitHub's command line tool.

New personal repos do not let workflows open pull requests. You allow it once, under Settings, Actions, General, Workflow permissions.

The second way is [Argo CD Image Updater](https://github.com/argoproj-labs/argocd-image-updater), a separate add-on. It watches your registry, the online store that holds your images. When a version that matches your rule appears, it writes the new tag for you. You configure it with its own custom resource (a new kind of Kubernetes object), `ImageUpdater`. The lab's optional `argocd/image-updater.yaml` is one.

With the `git` write-back method, Image Updater commits straight to the branch, with no pull request and no signature. Its README says it is under active development and not yet recommended for critical production workloads.

My advice: start with the CI pull request for every environment. If the dev pull requests turn into busywork, let Image Updater handle dev, and keep prod on pull requests.

New versions now reach git cleanly. Next, we'll control the order in which one sync applies things.

sections.h: Putting things in order: sync waves and hooks
sections.body:
A kitchen does not cook everything at once. The stock goes on first, the sauce waits for the stock, and someone tastes the dish before it leaves. A sync, Argo CD's act of applying git to the cluster, has the same needs. Argo CD already applies Namespaces first, then other built-in kinds, then custom resources. Sometimes you need more control. Redis, the small database that counts the visits, should be ready before the app starts. Or a database migration, a script that changes how stored data is laid out, must finish before new code arrives.

A sync wave is an annotation on any object: `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"`. An annotation is a note on an object that tools can read. Argo CD applies the lowest wave first and waits until it is in sync and healthy before it starts the next. Objects without the annotation are in wave 0, and negative numbers are allowed.

A hook is an object that runs at a set point of the sync. It is usually a Job: an object that runs a Pod until its command finishes, instead of keeping it running. You mark it with the annotation `argocd.argoproj.io/hook`:
- `PreSync` runs before anything is applied. If it fails, the sync stops. Use it for a database migration.
- `Sync` runs together with the normal objects.
- `PostSync` runs after everything is applied and Healthy. Use it for a smoke test.
- `SyncFail` runs when the sync fails, for clean-up or an alert.

A smoke test is a quick check that the app answers at all: tasting the soup. The lab's `gitops/smoke-test.yaml` is a PostSync hook. It calls `/healthz`, the app's "are you alive?" address, once with curl, a tool that fetches a web address. If curl gets an error, Argo CD marks the sync as failed, and you see it in the web page. A second annotation, `argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy`, decides when Argo CD deletes the finished Job.

One catch: hooks do not run during a selective sync, when you sync only some of an app's objects. Sync the whole app when you want the hooks.

Next comes the one kind of file that must never sit in git as plain text.

sections.h: Keeping secrets out of a GitOps repo
sections.body:
Every restaurant has a safe, and nobody writes its code on the board that every cook and driver can read. A GitOps repo has the same problem. Anyone with access to the repo can read everything in it, and git keeps every old version.

A plain Kubernetes Secret, the object that holds passwords and keys, is only base64 encoded (Day 42). Base64 writes any data as plain letters, and anyone can turn it back. So committing a Secret is the same as committing the password.

Three tools solve this. The first uses a key pair: a public key that can only lock, and a matching private key that is the only way to open the lock again.
- Sealed Secrets: you encrypt a Secret on your laptop with `kubeseal` and the cluster's public key, then commit the result, a SealedSecret. Only the controller in that cluster holds the private key that turns it back into a Secret.
- External Secrets Operator: git holds only a pointer, an ExternalSecret that names an entry in a store such as AWS Secrets Manager or Vault. The operator copies the value into a Secret in the cluster.
- SOPS: encrypts the values inside a YAML file with a key from age (a small encryption tool) or a cloud key service. The keys of the file stay readable; the values do not.

Argo CD's [secret management](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/secret-management/) page strongly recommends the styles where the Secret is created in the destination cluster, such as the first two. Then Argo CD never sees the value. It cautions against plugins that inject secrets while Argo CD renders the YAML, because those values then sit in Argo CD's Redis cache in plain text.

**A password in git is no longer a secret. Commit only locked secrets, or pointers to them.**

hello-devops has no real secrets yet, so the lab needs none of this today. Day 64 goes deeper into secrets, access and policy.

The last question is who may change which board, and whether Argo CD is the only tool for the job.

sections.h: Who may change what, and the other GitOps tool, Flux
sections.body:
The manager of the test kitchen may change the test kitchen's board, but not the main room's. Argo CD draws those lines with projects. Everything last time used the `default` project, which allows any repo, any cluster, any namespace and any kind of object. An AppProject narrows that down for a group of apps. The lab's `argocd/project.yaml` allows:
- One source repo: yours.
- Three namespaces in the local cluster: `hello`, `hello-dev` and `hello-prod`.
- No cluster-wide objects except Namespaces.

Point an app in this project at another repo, or at `kube-system`, where Kubernetes keeps its own parts, and Argo CD refuses to sync it. Projects also hold roles: the lab's `viewer` role may look at the apps and read logs, nothing more.

Who may do what in the web page and CLI is set by Argo CD's own RBAC, rules that give each role its permissions. It is separate from Kubernetes RBAC (Day 46). A fresh install has one user, `admin`, who may do everything. Teams connect single sign-on, so people log in with their work account, and map groups to roles such as the built-in `role:readonly`.

[Flux](https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2) is the other big GitOps tool. Like Argo CD it is a graduated CNCF project, which means the foundation behind Kubernetes rates it as mature. The ideas from these two lessons carry over. The differences are mostly about style:
- Flux is a set of small controllers that you drive with YAML and the `flux` CLI. Its core has no web UI; the separate [Flux Operator](https://fluxoperator.dev/web-ui/) adds one.
- Flux usually runs inside every cluster it manages, while one Argo CD often manages many clusters from one place.
- Flux ships its own image automation controllers and can decrypt SOPS files itself; Argo CD uses Image Updater and plugins.

Choose Argo CD when people want a web page to see and sync apps. Choose Flux when the team wants everything as YAML and no central server.

Both tools stop at the same place. They make sure the cluster runs what git says. A Synced, Healthy app can still be slow, or fail for one user in ten. Seeing that needs a different set of tools, and the next part starts building them.

worked.title: Promote 1.1.0 from dev to prod by hand

steps.say: Ask git, not the cluster, what each environment should run. `kubectl kustomize` builds an overlay's final YAML on your laptop and never touches the cluster. Dev already runs 1.1.0, and prod still runs 1.0.0. Both are local images in your kind cluster.
steps.code:
$ kubectl kustomize overlays/dev | grep 'image:'
        image: hello-devops:1.1.0
      - image: redis:8-alpine
$ kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | grep 'image:'
        image: hello-devops:1.0.0
      - image: redis:8-alpine

steps.say: Try `kustomize edit set image` first. It sets the tag, but look at the size of the change: it rewrote the whole file. Comments at line ends are gone, and lists are re-indented. A reviewer would have to hunt for the one line that matters, so throw that edit away.
steps.code:
$ cd overlays/prod
$ kustomize edit set image hello-devops:1.1.0
$ cd ../..
$ git diff --stat
 overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml | 80 ++++++++++++++++++++--------------------
 1 file changed, 40 insertions(+), 40 deletions(-)
$ git checkout -- .

steps.say: `yq` changes only the field you name and keeps everything else, comments included. Now the diff is one line, and the review takes seconds. (`-U1` shows one line of context instead of three.)
steps.code:
$ yq -i '(.images[] | select(.name == "hello-devops")).newTag = "1.1.0"' \
    overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
$ git diff -U1
diff --git a/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml b/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
index dc5f3ef..f0ec01f 100644
--- a/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
+++ b/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
@@ -15,3 +15,3 @@ images:
   - name: hello-devops
-    newTag: "1.0.0" # prod runs the release that already passed dev
+    newTag: "1.1.0" # prod runs the release that already passed dev
 replicas:

steps.say: Check the result before you commit: build prod's YAML again and confirm the new tag. This catches a typo before Argo CD ever sees it.
steps.code:
$ kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | grep 'image:'
        image: hello-devops:1.1.0
      - image: redis:8-alpine

steps.say: Ship it like any other change: a branch, a commit and a pull request. Argo CD watches only `main`, so nothing deploys until someone reviews and merges.
steps.code:
$ git switch -c promote/prod-1.1.0
$ git commit -am "Promote hello-devops 1.1.0 to prod"
$ git push -u origin promote/prod-1.1.0
$ gh pr create --fill
$ gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch

steps.say: Within about three minutes Argo CD syncs `hello-devops-prod`, and the rollout replaces the four prod Pods one at a time. Dev was not touched, because its folder did not change. If prod misbehaves, press Revert on the merged pull request and merge the revert: Argo CD puts 1.0.0 back.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello-prod get deployment hello-devops \
    -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'
hello-devops:1.1.0

code.title: argocd/project.yaml
code.src:
# An Argo CD project: the rules for every hello-devops Application (Day 48).
# It says which repo the apps may read, where they may deploy, and which
# cluster-wide objects they may create. Apply it before applicationset.yaml:
#   kubectl apply -n argocd -f argocd/project.yaml
# Replace <your-github-user> with your GitHub user name first.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: hello
  namespace: argocd
  # Argo CD will not delete this project while an Application still uses it.
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
spec:
  description: hello-devops in dev and prod
  # Apps in this project may only read your repo.
  sourceRepos:
    - https://github.com/<your-github-user>/hello-devops
  # They may only deploy to these namespaces of the cluster Argo CD runs in.
  # (hello is for the Day 47 app, if you move it into this project.)
  destinations:
    - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
      namespace: hello
    - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
      namespace: hello-dev
    - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
      namespace: hello-prod
  # Cluster-wide objects are denied, except Namespaces (the app creates its own).
  clusterResourceWhitelist:
    - group: ""
      kind: Namespace
  # A role you can hand out later, for example to a teammate or a dashboard:
  # it can look at the apps and read their logs, but not sync or delete them.
  roles:
    - name: viewer
      description: Read-only access to hello-devops apps
      policies:
        - p, proj:hello:viewer, applications, get, hello/*, allow
        - p, proj:hello:viewer, logs, get, hello/*, allow

# An ApplicationSet: one template that makes one Argo CD Application per
# environment (Day 48). Here it makes hello-devops-dev and hello-devops-prod.
# Each one deploys a Kustomize overlay from your repo into its own namespace.
# Apply it after project.yaml:
#   kubectl apply -n argocd -f argocd/applicationset.yaml
# Replace <your-github-user> with your GitHub user name first.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  # Use Go templates ({{.env}}) and stop with an error on a misspelled name.
  goTemplate: true
  goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]
  # The generator makes one set of values per environment.
  generators:
    - list:
        elements:
          - env: dev
            namespace: hello-dev
          - env: prod
            namespace: hello-prod
  # The template is a normal Application with {{.env}} and {{.namespace}} filled in.
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "hello-devops-{{.env}}"
      labels:
        env: "{{.env}}"
    spec:
      project: hello # the rules in project.yaml
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/<your-github-user>/hello-devops
        targetRevision: main
        path: "overlays/{{.env}}" # the Kustomize overlay for this environment (Day 45)
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: "{{.namespace}}"
      # Same reason as in application.yaml: the autoscaler owns the replica count.
      ignoreDifferences:
        - group: apps
          kind: Deployment
          name: hello-devops
          jsonPointers:
            - /spec/replicas
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true # delete things that you removed from git
          selfHeal: true # undo changes made by hand in the cluster
        syncOptions:
          - CreateNamespace=true
          - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true

code.title: .github/workflows/bump-image.yml
code.src:
# Opens a pull request that changes which image version one environment runs (Day 48).
# Save it as .github/workflows/bump-image.yml in your repo. (This reference copy
# sits in gitops/ so that it never runs in the course's own repo.)
# Once, before the first run: Settings > Actions > General > Workflow permissions,
# tick "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests".
# Run it from the Actions tab, or with:
#   gh workflow run bump-image.yml -f environment=dev -f version=1.2.0
name: bump-image

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        description: Which environment to change
        type: choice
        options: [dev, prod]
        default: dev
      version:
        description: Image tag to deploy, such as 1.2.0 (no "v" in front)
        type: string
        required: true

# Only what this job needs: push a branch and open a pull request.
permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write

# One bump per environment at a time.
concurrency:
  group: bump-image-${{ inputs.environment }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  bump:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    env:
      # Inputs go through env variables, never straight into a script.
      ENVIRONMENT: ${{ inputs.environment }}
      VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }}
      FILE: overlays/${{ inputs.environment }}/kustomization.yaml
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Check the inputs
        run: |
          if [[ ! "$VERSION" =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]]; then
            echo "::error::Version must look like 1.2.0, got '$VERSION'"
            exit 1
          fi
          if [ -z "$(yq '.images[] | select(.name == "hello-devops") | .name' "$FILE")" ]; then
            echo "::error::$FILE has no images entry named hello-devops"
            exit 1
          fi

      # yq (already installed on GitHub's ubuntu runners) changes only these two
      # fields and keeps every comment. `kustomize edit set image` does the same
      # job, but it rewrites the whole file and drops comments at line ends.
      - name: Write the new image into the overlay
        run: |
          # The same lower case image name that release.yml pushes to.
          export IMAGE="ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}"
          yq -i '(.images[] | select(.name == "hello-devops")) |=
            (.newName = strenv(IMAGE) | .newTag = strenv(VERSION))' "$FILE"
          git diff

      - name: Open a pull request
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          if git diff --quiet; then
            echo "The $ENVIRONMENT overlay already uses $VERSION. Nothing to do."
            exit 0
          fi
          BRANCH="bump/${ENVIRONMENT}-${VERSION}"
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git switch -c "$BRANCH"
          git commit -am "Deploy hello-devops ${VERSION} to ${ENVIRONMENT}"
          git push origin "$BRANCH"
          gh pr create --base main --head "$BRANCH" \
            --title "Deploy hello-devops ${VERSION} to ${ENVIRONMENT}" \
            --body "Sets the hello-devops image in ${FILE}. Argo CD deploys it after you merge."
          {
            echo "### Pull request opened"
            echo "Branch \`$BRANCH\` sets $ENVIRONMENT to $VERSION."
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

code.title: gitops/smoke-test.yaml
code.src:
# A PostSync hook (Day 48): after every sync, once all resources are Healthy,
# Argo CD runs this Job. If curl fails, Argo CD marks the sync as failed.
# To try it, copy this file into overlays/dev/ and add
# "- smoke-test.yaml" to the resources list in that kustomization.yaml.
# The overlay moves it into namespace hello-dev, next to the hello-devops Service.
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: smoke-test
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PostSync
    # Delete the old Job just before the next sync creates a new one.
    # Until then you can still read its logs.
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0 # one try only: a failure fails the sync
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: curl
          image: curlimages/curl:8.22.0
          # -f: fail on an HTTP error, -sS: quiet but show errors, -m 5: give up after 5 seconds.
          # hello-devops is the Service name in this namespace, on port 80.
          args: ["-fsS", "-m", "5", "http://hello-devops/healthz"]
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 10m
              memory: 16Mi
            limits:
              memory: 32Mi

code.title: argocd/image-updater.yaml (optional)
code.src:
# OPTIONAL (Day 48): let Argo CD Image Updater move dev to each new release.
# You only need this file if you install Argo CD Image Updater (see its docs).
# It watches your image in GHCR and, when a higher 1.x version appears,
# commits the new image into overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml on main.
# It commits straight to main, with no pull request, so keep it to dev.
# Before you apply it:
#   1. Replace <your-github-user> below.
#   2. Create a Secret named git-creds in namespace argocd with two keys:
#      username (your GitHub user) and password (a fine-grained token that can
#      write to the hello-devops repo only).
# Apply it with: kubectl apply -n argocd -f argocd/image-updater.yaml
apiVersion: argocd-image-updater.argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ImageUpdater
metadata:
  name: hello-devops-dev
  namespace: argocd # the namespace of the Applications it updates
spec:
  # Write the new tag to git, using the token in the git-creds Secret.
  # (The default method, argocd, changes only the Application in the cluster.)
  writeBackConfig:
    method: git:secret:git-creds
    gitConfig:
      branch: main
      # Edit the overlay's kustomization.yaml, as `kustomize edit set image` would.
      writeBackTarget: kustomization
  applicationRefs:
    - namePattern: hello-devops-dev # only the dev Application
      images:
        - alias: app
          # ":1.x" is a version rule: any 1.something version, never 2.0.0.
          imageName: ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/hello-devops:1.x
          commonUpdateSettings:
            updateStrategy: semver # pick the highest version that fits the rule
            # Dev may still run the image that kind loaded (hello-devops:1.1.0),
            # which has a different name, so update even if no GHCR image runs yet.
            forceUpdate: true
          manifestTargets:
            kustomize:
              name: hello-devops # the image name in k8s/deployment.yaml

A PostSync smoke test fails the sync if checkout stops answering.

task.title: Run dev and prod from one ApplicationSet
steps: Add `argocd/project.yaml` and `argocd/applicationset.yaml` with your GitHub user name. Commit, push, and apply both. Last time's app can stay, because the overlays use ClusterIP Services.

Check that `hello-devops-dev` and `hello-devops-prod` appear and both turn Synced and Healthy. Dev uses the local image `hello-devops:1.1.0`; if kind lacks it, run `kind load docker-image hello-devops:1.1.0 --name devops`.
Port-forward to the dev and the prod Service in turn, and check with curl that each one greets you differently.
Add `.github/workflows/bump-image.yml`, push it, and allow workflows to create pull requests in the repo settings.
Push a new release tag, for example `v1.2.0`, and wait for `release.yml` to finish. Make the package public in GHCR (GitHub's image store), so kind can pull it without a password.
Run the bump workflow for dev with version `1.2.0`. Read the pull request: it should change two lines in `overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml`. Merge it.
Confirm that dev now runs `ghcr.io/<you>/hello-devops:1.2.0` while prod still runs its old tag.
Promote: run the workflow again for prod with the same version, merge, and confirm that both environments match.
Optional: add the smoke-test hook to the dev overlay, then break its URL and watch the dev sync fail.
hints: Checks may not start on their own for a pull request that the workflow opened with `GITHUB_TOKEN`; GitHub does this to stop workflow loops. If the merge box asks you to approve the workflow runs, approve them.
ImagePullBackOff after a bump usually means the GHCR package is still private, or the tag does not exist. `kubectl -n hello-dev describe pod` names the exact image it tried.
Unsure what a bump will change? Save the output of `kubectl kustomize overlays/dev` to a file before and after, then compare the two with `diff`.
task.done_when: You are done when the jsonpath command from the Commands list prints the same `ghcr.io/.../hello-devops:1.2.0` image for `hello-dev` and `hello-prod`, and both apps are Synced and Healthy.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate, in 3 to 4 sentences, how version 1.3.0 travels from a git tag to prod in this setup. Mention who builds the image, what changes in git, and what Argo CD does.
explain_back.answer: Pushing the tag v1.3.0 starts release.yml, which builds the image once and pushes it to GHCR as 1.3.0. A workflow then opens a pull request that sets the dev overlay to 1.3.0. After the merge, Argo CD sees the commit and deploys dev. When dev looks good, a second pull request copies the same tag into the prod overlay, someone reviews it, and Argo CD deploys prod. If prod breaks, reverting that pull request puts the old tag back.

recap: Deployment YAML lives in git, in the app repo or in a separate config repo with cleaner history and access.
Each environment gets one overlay and one Application; an ApplicationSet writes the Applications from one template.
Promotion is a pull request that copies a tested, fixed tag to the next overlay. Never deploy latest.
CI writes the new tag with a small edit (yq rather than kustomize edit set image) and opens a pull request; Image Updater can do it for dev.
Sync waves order objects, hooks run Jobs before or after a sync, and secrets stay out of git as Sealed or External Secrets.
AppProjects limit what apps may touch, and Flux is the main alternative. Neither tool can tell you whether users are happy.

check.q: You add `env: staging, namespace: hello-staging` to the list generator and create `overlays/staging`. The new app appears but never syncs. Why?
options: The hello project does not allow the hello-staging namespace
An ApplicationSet can make at most two Applications
Staging needs its own Argo CD install to work
The overlay folder must be named stage, not staging
check.why: The AppProject lists the places its apps may deploy to, so you also have to add hello-staging to project.yaml.

check.q: Image Updater runs with the lab's settings and finds a new version 1.4.0. What appears in your repo?
options: A pull request that waits for your review
Nothing; it patches only the live Deployment
A new git tag v1.4.0 on the main branch
A commit on main that changes the dev kustomization
check.why: With git write-back and the kustomization target, it commits straight to the branch Argo CD watches, with no pull request.

check.q: A Job marked `argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync` runs a database migration and fails. What happens to the new app version?
options: Argo CD applies it anyway and marks the sync failed
The sync stops before the other objects are applied
Argo CD retries the Job until the migration passes
The Job is skipped and the sync carries on as usual
check.why: A failed PreSync hook stops the whole sync, so new code never meets data in the old layout.

interview.q: How do you promote a release between environments with GitOps?
interview.a: CI builds the image once and tags it with a version, never latest. Each environment has its own folder, for example a Kustomize overlay. Promotion is a pull request that copies the tested tag or digest from one folder to the next. The review is the approval, and the merge is the deploy, because Argo CD or Flux syncs the change. Rolling back is a revert of that pull request.

interview.q: How do you handle secrets when everything lives in git?
interview.a: I never commit plain Secrets, because base64 is not encryption and git keeps history forever. One option is to commit encrypted SealedSecrets that only the controller in the cluster can decrypt. The other is to commit ExternalSecret references and let the External Secrets Operator fetch the values from a store such as Vault or AWS Secrets Manager. Argo CD recommends these styles, where the Secret is made in the destination cluster. I avoid plugins that inject secrets while Argo CD renders manifests, because those values land in its cache.

interview.q: When would you choose Flux over Argo CD?
interview.a: Both are graduated CNCF projects that pull from git and reconcile, so the core idea is the same. I would pick Argo CD when people want a web UI to see app health and sync by hand, or when one central install should manage many clusters. I would pick Flux when the team prefers everything as YAML and the CLI, runs one set of controllers per cluster, and wants image automation and SOPS decryption built in. Either way, the repo layout and promotion flow look much the same.

deeper.body:
Your setup is one cluster with two namespaces. A company with fifty clusters uses the same ideas, only generated.

Start with the generator. The list generator is only one of several; others read their list from folders in a git repo, from the clusters Argo CD knows, or from open pull requests. The cluster generator makes one Application per cluster. It can filter by labels on those clusters, such as `env: prod` or `region: eu`. Register a new cluster with the right labels, and every matching ApplicationSet deploys to it. The [Argo CD docs on cluster bootstrapping](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/cluster-bootstrapping/) recommend exactly this for new clusters. The matrix generator combines two generators, for example every folder under `apps/` times every cluster labelled `env: dev`.

Then decide where Argo CD itself runs:
- Hub and spoke: one Argo CD in a management cluster deploys to all the others. You get one UI and one place for access rules. If the hub is down, nothing new deploys, though running apps keep running.
- One Argo CD per cluster: no single point of failure, but more installs to upgrade. This is also the usual Flux model.

Changing fifty clusters at once is risky. ApplicationSet Progressive Syncs, a Beta feature, update the generated apps in steps. For example, dev clusters go first, then a few prod clusters, then the rest, and each step waits until the previous one is healthy.

Promotion itself can be automated too. Tools such as [Kargo](https://github.com/akuity/kargo) and [GitOps Promoter](https://github.com/argoproj-labs/gitops-promoter) run the promotion steps for you: they open the pull requests, wait for checks, and move a version from stage to stage.

Next, the rendered manifests pattern. With overlays and charts, a one-line change in a base can change the YAML of every environment, and the pull request does not show it. The Source Hydrator (Beta since Argo CD 3.5, off by default) renders each environment, commits the plain YAML to a separate branch, and syncs from there. Reviewers then read the exact YAML that will run, and `git diff` between two commits shows exactly what changed in prod.

You can get a cheap version of this today. In a pull request check, run `kubectl kustomize` for each overlay on both the main branch and the pull request branch, and post the diff as a comment. A reviewer who sees "prod: replicas 3 to 6" catches mistakes that "k8s/deployment.yaml: one line changed" hides.

Why does deleting an ApplicationSet remove so much? The controller marks each Application as owned by the set. It also adds the finalizer from last time's `application.yaml`. A finalizer is a note that makes Kubernetes run a clean-up step before it removes an object, and this one deletes an app's objects together with the app.

Keeping one repo has a small cost: a commit that changes only `overlays/` still runs `ci.yml` on main. If that bothers you, add `overlays/**` to the `paths-ignore` list of its push trigger, the list of folders whose changes should not start it.

One small timing detail: between sync waves, Argo CD pauses for 2 seconds.

Last, two access defaults changed in Argo CD 3.x, and older guides get them wrong. The right to update or delete an Application no longer covers the objects inside it. And reading Pod logs needs its own `logs` permission.

lessons.opening:
Picture the restaurant from last time, now with a second room. The owner has opened a small test kitchen next door, where new dishes are tried on a few regulars before they reach the main dining room. On Tuesday a new soup is a hit there. On Friday the main kitchen cooks it from memory: a little more salt, a different stock. The regulars ask why it tastes wrong.

The trap is easy to fall into, because it really feels like the same soup. Same name, same pot, same cooks. Last time, a board on the wall and a careful manager kept one room in step with git. That left an open question: how do you run two rooms from one board, and move a dish from one to the other without it changing on the way?

In this lesson, we'll run hello-devops as two copies, try a version in one, and move that exact version to the other with a reviewed change in git.

Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

aside.title: What is "app of apps", which so many blog posts use?
aside.body: It is one parent Application whose folder holds only other Application files. Argo CD deploys the parent, and the parent deploys the children. It came before ApplicationSets, and it still works. The Argo CD docs recommend ApplicationSets for most cases. They call app of apps an admin-only tool, because anyone who can push to that folder can create apps in any project.

lessons.closing:
We started with a soup that changed on its way from the test kitchen to the main room. Now one board template serves both rooms, and a dish moves only as a signed card: a pull request that copies the exact tag dev already ran. In your lab, open `overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml` and check that its tag is a real version, never `latest`.

Next, we'll stop asking whether the cluster runs what git says, and start asking a harder question: is the app actually working well for the people who use it?

recap: GitOps: git holds what should run, and a program in the cluster pulls it and keeps the cluster equal to it.
Pull deploys keep cluster keys out of CI, and every deploy becomes a commit you can review and revert.
Argo CD 3.x installs with server-side apply and marks the objects it owns with an annotation.
Sync status (does it match git?) and health (does it work?) are two separate signals.
Self-heal and prune are off by default. Tell Argo CD to ignore fields that another controller owns.
Roll back with git revert, or the Revert button on the pull request.
Each environment gets one overlay and one Application, and an ApplicationSet writes the Applications.
Promotion copies a tested, fixed image tag to the next environment through a pull request.
Secrets stay out of git with Sealed Secrets, External Secrets or SOPS; AppProjects and roles limit who deploys where.

flashcards.front: What are the four OpenGitOps principles?
flashcards.back: Declarative; versioned and immutable; pulled automatically; continuously reconciled.

flashcards.front: Push deploy or pull deploy: which one needs a cluster key in CI?
flashcards.back: Push. In a pull deploy, a program inside the cluster fetches from git and applies.

flashcards.front: Why does installing Argo CD 3.x need kubectl apply --server-side?
flashcards.back: The ApplicationSet definition is too big for the annotation that normal (client-side) apply writes.

flashcards.front: Sync status or health status: which one asks "does it work?"
flashcards.back: Health. Sync status asks whether the cluster matches git.

flashcards.front: What does selfHeal do, and is it on by default?
flashcards.back: It undoes changes made in the cluster but not in git. It is off by default.

flashcards.front: What does prune do, and is it on by default?
flashcards.back: It deletes objects you removed from git. It is off by default.

flashcards.front: How does Argo CD 3.x remember which app owns an object?
flashcards.back: With the annotation argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id on that object.

flashcards.front: How often does Argo CD check git by default?
flashcards.back: About every 3 minutes (120 s plus up to 60 s of random delay). A webhook makes it immediate.
So Argo CD and the autoscaler do not fight over the number of copies.

flashcards.front: How do you roll back an app that Argo CD syncs automatically?
flashcards.back: Revert the commit or pull request in git. Argo CD then deploys the old state.
A template plus generators that write many Applications, for example one per environment.
A pull request that copies a tested image tag from one environment's folder to the next.

flashcards.front: Why never deploy the latest tag with GitOps?
flashcards.back: Git does not change when the image does, so you cannot see or revert what runs.

flashcards.front: What does kustomize edit set image do, and what is the catch?
flashcards.back: It sets an image name and tag in the kustomization.yaml of the current folder, but rewrites the whole file and drops comments at line ends.

flashcards.front: When does a PostSync hook run?
flashcards.back: After all objects are applied and Healthy. A quick smoke test is a typical use.

flashcards.front: Which secret styles does Argo CD recommend?
flashcards.back: Ones that create the Secret inside the cluster, such as Sealed Secrets or External Secrets Operator.
Which repos, clusters, namespaces and kinds of objects its apps may use.

flashcards.front: What is the main style difference between Flux and Argo CD?
flashcards.back: Flux: small controllers in each cluster, driven by YAML and its CLI. Argo CD: often one central server with a web UI.

quiz.q: Automated sync is on and selfHeal is off. A teammate edits the live ConfigMap by hand. What do you see in Argo CD?
options: The edit is undone within a few seconds
The app shows OutOfSync, and the edit stays for now
The app shows Degraded until someone syncs it
Argo CD commits the edit into git for you
quiz.why: Without self-heal, a change in the cluster does not start a sync. Argo CD reports the drift, and the edit stays until the next commit is synced.

quiz.q: Which Argo CD part turns your Kustomize folder into plain YAML?
options: The application controller
The API server
The repository server
The Dex server
quiz.why: The repo server copies the repo and builds the YAML from Kustomize or Helm; the controller then compares and applies it.

quiz.q: You follow an old video and run plain `kubectl apply -n argocd -f install.yaml`. It fails on the ApplicationSet definition. What is the fix?
options: Add --server-side --force-conflicts to the apply
Install an older Kubernetes version in kind
Delete the ApplicationSet definition from the file
Run the same command again until it passes
quiz.why: That definition is too big for the annotation that client-side apply writes, and server-side apply does not write it.

quiz.q: After a tag change in git, your app stays Synced and Progressing for many minutes. What is the most likely cause?
options: Argo CD cannot reach the git repository
Self-heal is fighting with the autoscaler
The project forbids the destination namespace
The new Pods cannot start, for example the image cannot be pulled
quiz.why: Synced means the cluster has what git says. A rollout that never finishes points at the new Pods themselves.

quiz.q: Why does promotion copy the same image tag to prod instead of building a fresh image for prod?
options: GHCR allows only one push per version
Prod then runs exactly the bytes that were tested in dev
Building twice would cost extra GitHub Actions minutes only
Argo CD cannot deploy images built from a branch
quiz.why: Build once, deploy many: a rebuild could pick up new parts and ship something nobody tested.

quiz.q: Argo CD synced a new GREETING into hello-config, but curl still returns the old greeting. Why?
options: Argo CD has not pruned the old ConfigMap yet
The ConfigMap needs a sync wave of -1
The Pods read env variables only at start, so they need a restart
The Service still points at the old ReplicaSet
quiz.why: A container reads settings from a ConfigMap only when it starts. Restart the Deployment, or give the ConfigMap a new name.

quiz.q: How should a database password for hello-devops reach the cluster in a GitOps setup?
options: Commit an encrypted SealedSecret that only the cluster can decrypt
Commit a normal Secret, since base64 hides the value
Put it in the ConfigMap, then use a private repo
Type it with kubectl create secret and leave it out of git
quiz.why: A SealedSecret is safe in git and is unlocked only in the cluster. A Secret made by hand works, but it lives outside git and drifts.

quiz.q: You want a staging environment between dev and prod in this lab. What is the least you must add?
options: A second Argo CD install in a staging namespace
A copy of application.yaml for every Kubernetes object
A new branch called staging with its own k8s folder
An overlay folder, a generator entry, and the namespace in the project
quiz.why: The ApplicationSet makes the app from the new entry, the overlay holds its settings, and the project must allow the namespace.

quiz.q: Which statement about Flux and Argo CD is accurate?
options: Only Argo CD can deploy Kustomize overlays
Both pull from git and reconcile; Flux has image automation built in
Flux pushes changes from CI into the cluster
Argo CD is a CNCF project, while Flux is not
quiz.why: Both are graduated CNCF GitOps tools. Flux ships its own image automation; Argo CD uses the separate Image Updater.
